response:
**VERDICT: REVISE**

**Overall Assessment**: `TabsWidget` implements the static half of the WAI-ARIA APG Tabs pattern with unusual care — correct roles, correctly-synchronized `aria-selected`, correctly-paired `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby`, and roving-tabindex markup are all present and correct. But the keyboard interaction half of that same pattern was never built: there is no Arrow key handler, and because roving tabindex means only the currently-active tab carries `tabIndex={0}`, that omission is not a minor convenience gap — it makes every tab other than the initially active one unreachable by keyboard alone. This is confirmed by the driven keyboard trace in the evidence pack, not just by reading the source. (Evidence-scope note: the evidence pack also bundles ~30 `keyboard-a11y-tester` batch-crawl finding files for unrelated sibling pages — accordions, modals, forms, a data table, etc. — from the same crawl run. None of those concern `tabs-missing-arrow-nav.html`/`TabsWidget`, including the two similarly-named ones, `tabs-incomplete-aria-selected.json` and `tabbed-nav-vs-tab-pattern.json`, which are confirmed-distinct fixtures by URL and DOM-id convention (`#tab-1`/`#panel-1` vs. this component's `#tab-overview` etc.). Only `driven/tabs-missing-arrow-nav.trace.json` is in-scope hard evidence for this review; the rest is excluded from findings below. Full reasoning in Verdict Justification.)

**Pre-commitment Predictions**: Before reading the code, for a Tabs widget the likely defects are: (1) missing or incomplete Arrow key navigation, (2) `aria-selected` not synchronized with actual state, (3) tab panels missing `aria-labelledby` back-reference to their tab, (4) roving tabindex absent entirely (all tabs `tabIndex={0}` or all `-1`), (5) focus not managed when the active tab changes.

Actual: 4 of 5 predictions were clean. `aria-selected` toggles correctly and is confirmed announced by AT (trace `sr_announcement`). `aria-labelledby`/`aria-controls` cross-references resolve correctly. Roving-tabindex *markup* (`tabIndex={index === activeTab ? 0 : -1}`) is present and correctly derived from state. Only prediction (1) materialized — but it materialized in the most severe form that prediction can take: because roving tabindex was implemented as markup without the Arrow key mechanism that makes roving tabindex functional, tabs 2..N are not just "hard to navigate to," they are categorically unreachable via keyboard. I did not predict that specific compounding interaction going in; it only became clear once I traced the roving-tabindex mechanics against the confirmed absence of any Arrow key handler.

**Critical Findings** (blocks access):

1. **Arrow key navigation is entirely absent, and because roving tabindex leaves only the active tab in the Tab sequence, this makes every non-active tab unreachable by keyboard.** See `TabsWidget` component code (fixture under review), lines 17–22: `handleTabKeyDown` checks only `e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' '` — no `ArrowLeft`/`ArrowRight`/`Home`/`End` branch exists anywhere in the file. Combined with line 34, `tabIndex={index === activeTab ? 0 : -1}`, only one `<button role="tab">` is ever part of the native Tab order at a time. Native `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` cannot focus an element with `tabIndex={-1}` — that is standard, non-configurable browser focus-order behavior, not an implementation detail that could vary. With no Arrow key handler to call `.focus()` on a sibling tab and flip which one holds `tabIndex={0}`, there is no keyboard-operable path from the active tab to any other tab.
   - Confidence: HIGH. This is not inferred from source alone — the `keyboard-a11y-tester` driven trace (`evals/results/keyboard-a11y-tester/driven/tabs-missing-arrow-nav.trace.json`) tested exactly this against the live rendered page. `step_0001`: `Tab` lands on `#tab-overview` (`tabindex: 0`, `ax_name_role_state.states.selected: true`), with `sr_announcement.focus_announcement: "tab, Overview, selected, 1 control, position 1, set size 3"` — the AT correctly reports 3 tabs exist. `step_0002`: `ArrowRight` sent, same active element, `"focus_moved": false`, `"sr_announcement": {"new_phrases": [], "focus_announcement": null}`. `step_0003`: `ArrowLeft` sent, same active element again, `"focus_moved": false"`, again no announcement. Two independent Arrow key presses, against the real running component, produce zero effect — matching what the source predicts. This forecloses the most likely refutation ("maybe a parent element handles it") because the trace exercised the actual DOM, not the isolated JSX.
   - Which user group is impacted: Keyboard-only users and screen-reader users navigating the tablist per the AT-reported convention (both are blocked from reaching tab 2/3's panel content by any keyboard input). Not a low-vision or cognitive-only issue — this is an operability failure, not a legibility one.
   - Why this matters: The `sr_announcement` evidence shows the browser/AT tells the user "position 1, set size 3" — creating a correct expectation, per the WAI-ARIA APG Tabs pattern's Keyboard Interaction section, that Arrow keys move among the 3 tabs. Pressing them does nothing, silently. A keyboard-only user (motor-impaired, switch-device, or simply no mouse attached) has no way to view the content of tabs 2 or 3 at all — not "hard to find," but structurally unreachable, since the only alternative activation path (click) requires a pointing device this user category doesn't have. Per WCAG 2.1.1 (Keyboard) — "all functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface" — the tab-switching functionality itself fails this for 2 of 3 tabs. Per WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order), the roving-tabindex "order" collapses to a single stop instead of a traversable sequence. Per the WAI-ARIA APG Tabs pattern, Left/Right Arrow (for a horizontal tablist, which this is — no `aria-orientation` override, and none needed since horizontal is the default) is core required interaction for the "automatic activation" model this component already uses for click/Enter/Space.
   - Fix: Add a `keydown` handler on the tablist (or reuse/extend `handleTabKeyDown`) that intercepts `ArrowRight`/`ArrowLeft` (and, per the fuller APG pattern, `Home`/`End`), computes the next/previous tab index with wraparound at the ends, calls `.focus()` on that tab's button (a `ref` per tab, or `event.target.closest('[role="tablist"]')` + query), and calls `handleTabClick(nextIndex)` so `activeTab` state, `tabIndex`, `aria-selected`, and panel visibility move together atomically — matching the automatic-activation model already implied by the existing click behavior. The existing `Enter`/`Space` branch can stay (it is harmless, if redundant on a native `<button>`) but does not substitute for this: it can only ever re-activate whichever tab is *already* focused, since no other tab is ever reachable to receive Enter/Space in the first place.

**Major Findings** (significantly degrades experience): None. There is no second-tier ARIA, focus, or state-communication defect independent of the Critical finding above — the Home/End gap noted under "What's Missing" is a related but lower-order piece of the same root cause (incomplete keyboard-interaction handler), not a separate design problem, so it is folded into the fix above rather than listed as its own Major finding to avoid double-counting one underlying gap as two.

**Minor Findings** (friction but workaround exists):
- The `Enter`/`Space` branch in `handleTabKeyDown` (lines 18–21) is functionally inert scaffolding rather than a real keyboard-interaction implementation: on a native `<button>`, the browser already fires `onClick` for `Enter` and `Space` without any handler present, so this code only ever re-selects the tab that is already selected. It reads as a partial attempt at "keyboard support" that stops short of the part that matters (Arrow keys). Workaround: none needed on its own — it's harmless — but a developer skimming this code could mistakenly believe keyboard interaction is "handled" because a `handleTabKeyDown` function exists at all. Recommend removing it once the Arrow/Home/End handler subsumes it, or clearly commenting that it's redundant with native button semantics, so its presence doesn't mask the real gap on the next review pass.

**Enhancements** (best practice not met):
- Once the Arrow-key handler is added, extend it to `Home` (first tab) and `End` (last tab) per the fuller WAI-ARIA APG Tabs pattern. Not required for basic operability the way Left/Right is (Left/Right is the core mechanism; Home/End is a documented convenience on top of it), so this stays at Enhancement rather than folding into the Critical fix's minimum bar — but it's cheap to add in the same handler and completes the pattern.
- `.tab-button { transition: color 0.2s; }` is a trivial, non-essential transition well below any flashing/motion concern, but as a matter of consistent practice it costs little to gate it behind `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`. Not a WCAG failure at this magnitude — flagging as best-practice only.

**What's Missing** (gaps, unhandled edge cases, unstated assumptions):
- `Home`/`End` key support (see Enhancements) — absent, not implemented anywhere.
- Duplicate `tab.id` values are not defensively handled. `id={`tab-${tab.id}`}` / `id={`panel-${tab.id}`}` and their cross-references (`aria-controls`, `aria-labelledby`) all assume `tab.id` is unique within the `tabs` array. If the caller ever passes duplicate ids, two tabs/panels would collide on the same DOM id, breaking the ARIA reference resolution for a screen-reader user. I have no evidence this actually occurs (the trace's ids are unique — `overview`, etc.) — this is a props-contract assumption worth stating explicitly, not a proven defect.
- Behavior with an empty `tabs` array is unstated: the tablist would render with zero focusable children. Not evidenced either way; noted as an edge case, not a finding.
- 200%-zoom / reflow behavior is untested by the evidence pack (the driven trace is desktop-viewport only, 1280×800). The `[role="tablist"] { display: flex; gap: 4px; }` rule has no `flex-wrap`, so a larger tab count or narrower viewport than tested could overflow horizontally — but with 3 short labels at the tested viewport there is no evidence of an actual reflow problem. Flagged as an evidence gap, not a scored finding.

**Multi-Perspective Notes**:
- **Screen reader user**: Focus into the tablist is announced correctly and completely — role, name, selected state, and set position (`"tab, Overview, selected, 1 control, position 1, set size 3"`), which is exactly what the WAI-ARIA APG Tabs pattern and WCAG 4.1.2 require. But that same announcement sets an expectation ("set size 3") that Arrow keys will reach the other two tabs, and pressing them produces total silence — no announcement, no state change, no error. A screen-reader user following the standard convention hits a dead end with no feedback that anything went wrong, which is worse for discoverability than an audible failure would be.
- **Keyboard-only user**: This is where the Critical finding lands hardest. Tab order into and out of the widget is logical (tablist before panels, matching visual order), and the one reachable tab has a strong, visible focus indicator. But there is no way, with any sequence of keyboard input, to move focus onto tab 2 or tab 3 — Tab/Shift+Tab only ever land on whichever tab currently holds `tabIndex={0}`, and Arrow keys do nothing. Content behind non-active tabs is not "inconvenient to reach" — it is unreachable.
- **Low vision user (200% zoom, high contrast)**: Nothing evidenced here is a defect. The measured focus indicator (`outline: 3px solid #0066cc`, `outline-offset: 2px`) is present and, per the one clean contrast measurement in the trace (`step_0003`: `contrast: 5.56`, `aaa_pass: true`), well above the 3:1 minimum for non-text UI indicators (WCAG 2.4.7/1.4.11) — that measurement is discussed further in Verdict Justification because the trace is internally inconsistent about it across steps. Computed text contrast for both tab states (`#666` inactive, `#0066cc` active, both against a white/light background) is comfortably above 4.5:1 (≈5.7:1 and ≈5.6:1 respectively, by manual calculation from the declared hex values). The active tab's touch target measures 111×45 CSS px in the trace's bounding box, clearing the WCAG 2.5.8 24×24 minimum and the 44×44 recommendation on the height axis. Zoom/reflow itself is untested (see What's Missing) — not claimed as passing, just not evidenced as failing.
- **Cognitive accessibility**: The click-a-tab/see-a-panel interaction model is simple and conventional, with no destructive actions, timeouts, or error states in scope for this widget. The one relevant angle here is secondary to the Critical finding: a user who knows the "arrow keys move between tabs" convention and gets silent non-response on trying it may reasonably conclude the whole component is frozen or broken, which is a predictability/trust concern layered on top of the operability failure, not a separate defect.

*(Additional perspectives, briefer since none are HIGH- or MEDIUM-driven by anything beyond what's already covered above: Vestibular & motion — LOW; the only motion is a 0.2s color transition, far below any flashing or essential-motion concern. Auditory access — LOW/not applicable; no media elements exist in this component. Environmental contrast — LOW; the active state is signaled redundantly through color, font-weight, and a border, not color alone, satisfying WCAG 1.4.1, and the computed contrast ratios above clear the relevant thresholds.)*

| Perspective | Alarm Level | Trigger Signal |
|-------------|-------------|----------------|
| Screen reader | HIGH | Custom composite widget; AT correctly announces "set size 3" but the arrow-key convention that would let the user reach 2 of those 3 is completely non-functional (confirmed by trace). |
| Keyboard-only | HIGH | Same root cause, operability-framed: roving tabindex with no Arrow handler leaves only 1 of 3 tabs reachable by any keyboard input. |
| Low vision | MEDIUM | Standard interactive-widget checks apply (focus visibility, contrast, target size); measured evidence available and passing, but zoom/reflow untested. |
| Cognitive | MEDIUM | Standard widget with a secondary predictability concern (silent non-response to an expected convention), not a primary driver. |
| Vestibular & motion | LOW | Only a trivial, non-essential 0.2s color transition. No animation, parallax, or auto-play. |
| Auditory access | LOW | No media elements in this component. |
| Environmental contrast | LOW | Active state uses three redundant cues (color + weight + border); computed contrast ratios clear WCAG 1.4.3/1.4.11 thresholds. |

Screen reader and Keyboard-only are both HIGH — per the protocol, this component should be flagged for deep review via `/perspective-audit` once the Critical finding above is fixed, specifically to re-verify the fix against both perspectives together (an Arrow-key fix that only satisfies "focus moves" without re-announcing correctly to AT would just trade one gap for another).

**Verdict Justification**: One Critical finding, zero Major findings, and an otherwise carefully-built implementation is why this lands on REVISE rather than REJECT or ACCEPT-WITH-RESERVATIONS. REJECT would imply the underlying approach — native `<button>` elements, `role="tablist"`/`tab`/`tabpanel`, roving tabindex, paired `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` — is wrong; it isn't. It's exactly right, and Phase 2 (semantic HTML) and Phase 5 (state communication) both came back clean enough that I want to say so plainly rather than bury it: `aria-selected` is genuinely synchronized and AT-announced, not visual-only; panels use the native `hidden` attribute (removing them from the accessibility tree, not just hiding them visually) rather than relying on CSS alone; the native-HTML-first rule is respected throughout. ACCEPT-WITH-RESERVATIONS would understate the problem — a Critical, complete-access-blocking gap for two named user groups is not a "ship with reservations" situation. REVISE — fix the one well-scoped gap, then this is very close to done — fits.

*Severity calibration, stated explicitly per Phase 8:* the protocol's own worked example for this exact defect shape ("custom tabs with aria-selected but no arrow key navigation, focus doesn't cycle") is filed at MAJOR, and the `<Good>` example under `<Examples>` reaches the same MAJOR conclusion for a structurally similar description. I deliberately diverge from that baseline and file this at CRITICAL, because this specific implementation's mechanics go one step further than "arrow keys are missing as a convenience": the roving-tabindex markup being present-but-non-functional means the *only* keyboard path to any non-active tab is closed off entirely, not merely inconvenient. Realist Check: (1) realistic worst case is a keyboard-only or screen-reader-only user permanently unable to view 2 of 3 tabs' content, with no error or workaround available to them — not a minor inconvenience with an easy alternative path; (2) impacted groups are keyboard-only and screen-reader users specifically, i.e., exactly the groups this skill exists to protect; (3) detection in production would be slow — axe-core and other static scanners check ARIA attribute presence/validity, not Arrow-key behavior, so this class of defect is exactly what passes automated checks and ships; (4) the severity is proportional to a mechanically-traced, evidence-confirmed access loss, not inflated by review momentum — I found nothing else in this component to pad a verdict with, which is itself a signal I'm not defaulting to "component has a bug, therefore CRITICAL." Per the recalibration rule "NEVER downgrade findings that involve complete access loss," this could equally be read as "never *under*-grade" in spirit — I'm naming that this is a judgment call diverging from the protocol's generic illustrative example, specifically so a developer disagreeing with CRITICAL can see exactly where the disagreement would have to be (is "2 of 3 tabs are keyboard-unreachable" actually accurate for this code, given roving-tabindex semantics? I believe the trace evidence settles that it is) rather than a black-box severity label.

*Evidence-scope discipline, stated explicitly per Phase 0:* the evidence pack contains one artifact directly about the page under review (`driven/tabs-missing-arrow-nav.trace.json`) and roughly 30 `keyboard-a11y-tester` batch-crawl finding files for other pages generated in the same crawl run (accordion, app shell, async form, breadcrumb, button/skip-link, checkbox group, combobox, dashboard, data table, expandable section, file input, form-field-vs-summary, form validation, heading hierarchy, image carousel, infinite scroll, interactive dropdown ×2, loading state, mega menu, modal, multistep form, pagination, popover, radio group, search-focus, search-results, tabbed-nav-vs-tab-pattern, tabs-incomplete-aria-selected, toast, tooltip, video player). None of those files' URLs match `tabs-missing-arrow-nav.html`, and the two most confusable by name (`tabbed-nav-vs-tab-pattern.json`, `tabs-incomplete-aria-selected.json`) are verifiably different fixtures — different URLs, and DOM id conventions (`#tab-1`/`#panel-1`) that don't match this component's actual rendered ids (`#tab-overview`, confirmed in the driven trace). I have not used any finding from those sibling-page files as evidence for this review, and no finding above rests on them. This is worth stating explicitly rather than silently: a review that quietly absorbed findings like "missing accessible name on tabpanel" or "positive tabindex" from those sibling files into a review of `TabsWidget` would be citing evidence for a defect in the wrong component.

**Open Questions (unscored)**:
- The driven trace's `focus_appearance` measurement for `#tab-overview` is internally inconsistent across steps that should show the *same* state: `step_0001` and `step_0002` report `contrast: null`, `area_pass: false`, `aaa_pass: false`; `step_0003` — same element, same focus, `focus_moved: false` at every step so nothing about the element's actual rendering changed — reports `contrast: 5.56`, `area_pass: true`, `aaa_pass: true`. Manually computing the contrast of the declared CSS color (`#0066cc` outline, presumably against a white/light background) independently lands at ≈5.56–5.57:1, matching `step_0003`'s reading, not the `null`/`false` reading from `step_0001`/`step_0002`. My read is that `step_0001`'s `changed_area: 0` is a first-frame artifact (nothing to diff against on the very first focus event) and `step_0002` inherits the same no-change reading because nothing moved, while `step_0003` is where the tool's diff-based measurement actually resolved a value — i.e., an instrumentation/measurement-timing quirk in the trace, not a real change in the underlying CSS or a real intermittent contrast failure on a static, unchanged element. I have not filed this as a WCAG 2.4.13 finding because doing so would mean scoring a measurement gap as a defect when the one full reading available for this exact element passes AAA. Flagging this as an open question about the evidence itself, in case there's trace-generation context I'm missing that would explain the null/false readings as something other than a first-frame gap. (Also worth noting for calibration: WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance is a Level AAA criterion; the applicable AA requirement, 2.4.7 Focus Visible, only requires *a* visible indicator, which is unambiguously present here regardless of how this specific sub-question resolves.)
- Duplicate `tab.id` handling and empty-`tabs`-array behavior (see What's Missing) — no evidence either way; would need the caller's actual data or a targeted test to resolve.
- Zoom/reflow behavior at 200% and at viewport widths narrower than the tested 1280px — not covered by the evidence pack; recommend a follow-up pass with `keyboard-a11y-tester` or a manual check at mobile widths, particularly if `tabs` can grow beyond the 3 tested here.

_benchmark.method: Phase 3 evidence-volume lane, hosted arm: Agent(subagent_type=general-purpose, model=sonnet) spawned depth-1 from the main session; subagent read exactly two staged files — the frontmatter-stripped a11y-critic SKILL.md (system-prompt equivalent) and the composed user prompt built by run_evidence_lane.assemble_prompt (PROMPT_PREFIX + blind fixture + labeled evidence-pack block, byte-identical to the local arm per README §5.1) — with all other reads barred (evals/ answer keys explicitly); response written by the subagent verbatim to this row's .md sibling, wrapped to JSON by wrap_hosted_rows.py without modification.
